back2basics.text: Judicial recusal is when a judge abstains from hearing a case due to potential conflicts of interest or personal connections to parties involved, ensuring impartiality and fairness. This practice upholds public confidence in the judiciary by preventing bias or the appearance of bias in judicial proceedings.

2026-11-24-am-1de92abe76.deck: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant recused himself from a Supreme Court hearing on November 23, 2026, concerning stalled housing projects of Supertech Limited due to a personal acquaintance with one applicant. This development highlights judicial ethics and the ongoing legal process to resolve homebuyers' disputes in major urban real estate cases.

2026-11-24-am-68d8a6cc12.anchor: International climate negotiations and global environmental governance

back2basics.text: The Conference of Parties (COP) is an annual meeting of countries under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change to negotiate and coordinate global action on climate change. These summits aim to build consensus on emission reductions, climate finance, and adaptation strategies, but progress often faces challenges due to differing national interests and priorities.

2026-11-24-am-68d8a6cc12.deck: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended without consensus on a key political statement due to disagreements over fossil fuel language and climate finance. This matters for UPSC aspirants as it highlights challenges in international climate negotiations and the role of developed and developing countries, including India, in global environmental governance.

back2basics.concept: Poverty Eradication through Agriculture and Rural Development
back2basics.text: Poverty eradication involves improving income and living standards of the poor, especially in rural areas where agriculture is the main livelihood. Government schemes provide financial support, infrastructure, and technology to farmers and rural communities. Scientific research in agriculture enhances productivity and resilience. Rural development programs focus on housing, roads, employment, and empowerment of vulnerable groups like women. Coordinated efforts across ministries ensure these benefits reach the intended populations effectively.

2026-11-24-am-6b206b4b30.deck: A joint workshop chaired by Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan reviewed the contributions of agriculture and rural development sectors in reducing India's extreme poverty from 27.1% to 2.6%. This event underscored the importance of inter-ministerial coordination and scientific innovations in sustaining rural progress and targeting the remaining poor.

body.label: Watershed and land resource management

2026-11-24-am-93c058e86f.anchor: Digital public infrastructure and AI governance

back2basics.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems that can perform tasks requiring human intelligence, such as identifying patterns and making decisions. In governance, AI can analyze large data sets to identify eligible beneficiaries for welfare schemes, reduce errors and exclusion, and improve delivery efficiency. This supports inclusive development by ensuring government benefits reach all rightful recipients.

2026-11-24-am-93c058e86f.deck: The Chief Secretary of Karnataka urged the use of artificial intelligence to ensure government benefits reach all eligible citizens, especially the underprivileged and excluded groups. This highlights the role of AI in promoting inclusive governance and entitlement-based welfare delivery.

body: AI helps identify underprivileged and excluded groups such as persons with disabilities and families left out of housing and guarantee schemes.
It enables a shift from application-based to entitlement-based delivery, ensuring rightful beneficiaries receive benefits without procedural hurdles.
AI supports sustainability and good governance by reducing exclusion and improving targeting accuracy.
Challenges include data privacy, digital divide, and ensuring AI systems are transparent and accountable.
structure.conclusion: Harnessing AI in governance can significantly improve inclusive welfare delivery if implemented with safeguards.

back2basics.text: India’s neighbourhood policy involves fostering friendly relations, economic cooperation, and strategic partnerships with neighbouring countries. back2basics.concept: International Court of Justice and Genocide
back2basics.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations that settles disputes between states according to international law. Genocide is a crime defined by intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. The ICJ can rule on state responsibility for genocide but relies on the UN Security Council for enforcement, which can be blocked by veto powers.

2026-11-24-am-db94562763.deck: On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya community. This verdict is crucial for understanding international law on genocide, human rights enforcement, and the geopolitical complexities affecting justice.

body.text: The court noted past atrocities including mass expulsions in 1978 and 1991-92, citizenship denial in 1982, and systemic discrimination culminating in the 2017 violence.

back2basics.concept: Systemically Important Banks and Capital Buffers
back2basics.text: Systemically Important Banks are those whose failure could threaten the stability of the financial system. To mitigate this risk, regulators require these banks to maintain additional capital buffers beyond the minimum regulatory capital. The Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital is a key measure of a bank's financial strength, representing its core equity capital against risk-weighted assets. These buffers help ensure banks can absorb losses during financial stress, protecting depositors and the economy.

2026-11-24-am-f198330227.deck: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced the 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks, maintaining State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank as D-SIBs with specific additional capital requirements. Understanding this list is important for UPSC aspirants as it highlights the RBI's role in financial stability and regulatory frameworks relevant to the banking sector.

body.text: The RBI issued the Framework for D-SIBs in 2014 and updated it in 2023, requiring disclosure of D-SIBs and assigning them to buckets based on their Systemic Importance Scores.

body.label: Capital Buffer Requirements
body.text: These banks must maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital buffer over the capital conservation buffer, varying by bucket: SBI at 0.80%, HDFC Bank at 0.40%, and ICICI Bank at 0.20% of Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs).

body.label: Global Coordination

back2basics.text: Judicial review allows courts to examine the legality of decisions made by educational institutions, ensuring they comply with principles of natural justice and fairness. back2basics.concept: Mineral Concession Rules and Mining Plans
back2basics.text: Mineral Concession Rules regulate the grant of mining leases and prospecting licenses in India. Mining plans are detailed documents prepared by accredited agencies outlining how mining operations will be conducted, including extraction methods, environmental safeguards, and closure plans. These plans ensure scientific and sustainable mining practices and are prerequisites for operationalizing mining blocks.

2026-11-24-am-fd24f5b19d.deck: The Ministry of Coal issued new guidelines for mining and mine closure plans for coal and lignite mines and amended the Mineral Concession Rules to extend accreditation periods for key agencies. These reforms aim to streamline mining operations, improve regulatory efficiency, and support energy security, relevant for UPSC aspirants studying resource management and governance.

body.label: Guidelines issued
body.text: The Ministry of Coal issued the “Guidelines for preparation of Mining Plan and Mine Closure Plan for Coal and Lignite Mines, 2026” on 20 November 2026, effective 30 days later.

body.label: Framework purpose
body.text: These guidelines provide an outcome-oriented framework for systematic and scientific mine planning and closure, complementing existing statutory provisions and avoiding redundant compliance.

body.label: Time-bound processes
body.text: Defined timelines are set for scrutiny and approval stages, ensuring faster decision-making and reducing reimbursement time from escrow accounts for mine closure works to one month.

body.label: Technological recognition
body.text: The guidelines recognize Underground Coal Gasification as a mining method and include specific guidelines for its mining plan preparation and approval.

body.label: Operational flexibility
body.text: Project proponents are given greater flexibility aligned with prevailing conditions to enable faster operationalization of mines.

body.label: Expected impact
body.text: The guidelines aim to improve Ease of Doing Business, accelerate mine operationalization, support energy security, and promote scientific mine closure benefiting local communities.

sections.heading: What are the new guidelines for mining and mine closure plans?

body.label: Amendment notified
body.text: The Ministry of Coal notified the Mineral Concession (Third Amendment) Rules, 2026 on 17 November 2026.

body.label: Accreditation period extended
body.text: The accreditation cycle for Accredited Prospecting Agencies (APA) and Mining Plan Preparing Agencies (MPPA) has been extended from three to five years.

body.label: Benefits of extension
body.text: This reduces the frequency of assessments and re-accreditations, saving time and ensuring continuity in preparing geological reports and mining plans necessary for coal and lignite block operationalization.

body.label: Governance impact
body.text: The reform supports Ease of Doing Business and trust-based governance in the coal sector.
